Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 352 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2023) 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 352 is in West-Central Alberta, covering an area of 1873 km2. WMU 352 is 
bordered on the north by the Little Smoky River and on the south by the Berland River (Fig. 1). The WMU 
overlaps portions of both ranges for the Little Smoky and A La Peche woodland caribou populations. Ongoing 
wolf reductions in these areas have halted declines in these caribou populations, avoiding extirpation, until habitat 
restoration actions can eventually support self-sustaining populations. It is important to manage overabundant 
moose densities in the Little Smoky and A La Peche caribou ranges where predator control has reduced natural 
moose mortality, and populations would otherwise grow. An antlerless moose special license is available in this 
WMU. The objective of this survey (2023) is to update the population estimate and ratio for sex and age classes 
of moose since the last survey was completed in 2016.   
Survey Method 
The aerial survey for moose in WMU 352 was conducted between January 29th and 30th, 2023. Distance sampling 
methods (AEP 2016, Buckland et al., 2001) were used to determine moose population and density estimates.  
Transects (N = 157), up to 10 km in length and oriented North-South (Fig. 1), were established throughout the unit 
with 1.2 km spacing. Three factors of canopy cover (0-33%, 43-66%, and >66%) within 10 m of the moose were 
estimated for each moose observation to include as a covariate for the detection functions. Moose were classified 
by age, sex, and antler class (AEP 2010).  
Results 
Total survey effort included 1548.63 km of transects, and approximately 19.8 hours of flight time. In total, 166 
moose were included in the analysis from 106 independent group observations. A total of 161 moose were 
successfully classified, of which 82 were cows, 32 were calves, and 47 were bulls. Of the bulls observed, 89% 
had already shed their antlers. Of those with antlers (n=5), 3 were considered small (small spike or forked antlers) 
and 2 were considered medium (small palmated antler ‘paddles’).  
The bull:cow and calf:cow ratios were 0.57 (95% CI 0.40 - 0.75) and 0.39 (95% CI 0.29 – 0.49), respectively. The 
density estimate was 0.27 moose/km2 (90% CI 0.22 - 0.32) with a coefficient of variation (CV) of 11.29%. The 
estimated moose population for WMU 352 is 503 (90% CI 418 - 606). See Table 1 for a comparison to previous 
survey results. The moose population is estimated to have increased by 51.1% since 2016, representing an 
annual average population growth rate of 1.06 (90% CI 1.01-1.11).  
We also observed 11 white-tailed deer (1 doe, 1 fawn, 9 unclassified), 28 mule deer (2 does, 4 fawns, 3 bucks, 19 
unclassified), and 112 elk (23 cows, 13 calves, 6 bulls, 70 unclassified).
